turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Hey, thanks for jumping on this. So I was testing the new filter yesterday, and something felt a little off.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Sure, what were you seeing exactly?

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: When I select two filters together, like brand and price range, some products just disappear. Even products that should match both filters aren't showing up.

turns.speaker: Emily
turns.text: Does it happen with every combination of filters, or only specific ones?

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: It seems to happen mostly when I combine brand with price range. I haven't tested every possible combination yet.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Right, yeah. That's actually related to how the indexing currently works for combined attributes.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Okay, but why would it work that way? From a user's point of view, that looks like a bug.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: I understand. The filters are indexed separately, and when you combine them, the system relies on the indexed attribute combinations available at that point.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So the system isn't actually checking the product data in real time?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Correct. It's querying the search index rather than the product database directly.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: And that's why some valid products are missing?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Exactly. If the relevant attribute combination isn't represented correctly in the index, the product won't appear in the filtered result.

turns.speaker: Emily
turns.text: Is the product itself still available if you search for it without applying the filters?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Yes, in most cases. The product data itself isn't missing. The problem is with how the filter criteria are being applied to the indexed data.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Hmm, I don't fully follow, but would it be possible to change that?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Technically, yes, but it wouldn't be a small change. We'd need to review the indexing logic and potentially rebuild part of the indexer.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: How much of the search system would that affect?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Potentially quite a lot. The same indexing logic is used by category pages and search results, so we'd need to be careful not to improve filtering accuracy while making the overall search slower.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: So we're basically trading accuracy for performance?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Exactly. We could make the filtering more accurate, but depending on the implementation, category pages with a large number of products could become noticeably slower.

turns.speaker: Emily
turns.text: Do we have any numbers on the performance impact?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Not yet. I haven't tested the alternative implementation, so I don't want to guess.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Could we benchmark the current implementation against the proposed one?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Yes. That's actually what I'd recommend before making any decision.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Is there a reason we can't just test it on a few categories first?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: That's a reasonable approach. We could enable the alternative indexing logic for a limited set of categories and compare the results.

turns.speaker: Emily
turns.text: From QA's side, I'd prefer that. We could select categories with a large number of products and test several filter combinations.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: That would also give us some real performance data instead of relying on assumptions.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Exactly. We could monitor response time, index size, and the number of products returned for each filter combination.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: How many categories would you suggest for the initial test?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Maybe three or four. I'd choose one small category, one medium-sized category, and one or two large categories.

turns.speaker: Emily
turns.text: I'd also include categories with a lot of products sharing the same brand and price ranges. That should make the issue easier to reproduce.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Good point. Those categories would give us more useful data.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: What would happen if we just left it as is for now?

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Most users probably won't notice because the common single-filter scenarios still work. But the combined-filter issue could create confusing search results.

turns.speaker: Emily
turns.text: And it could be difficult for QA to treat it as a simple UI issue because the missing products are caused by backend indexing.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: So would you consider it a blocker?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: I wouldn't call it a blocker for the current release. The existing functionality still works for the majority of use cases.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I agree. But I'd definitely keep it on the backlog because it affects the accuracy of the filtering experience.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Okay. What would be the risk of leaving it unchanged for another sprint?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: The main risk is that users could assume products are unavailable when they're actually available. There's also a chance we'll have to explain inconsistent filter results to the client.

turns.speaker: Emily
turns.text: We should probably document the current behavior so QA doesn't report the same thing repeatedly as a new defect.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Good idea. We can mark it as a known limitation until we decide whether to change the indexing logic.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Alright. Just so I understand correctly: for now, nothing changes, but David will investigate a limited rollout?

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: That's right. I'll put together a quick estimate for the alternative approach and identify which categories would be suitable for testing.
